title: Scope of practice & direct access
blurb: What a dental nurse can do, which extra skills need training, the lines you never cross, and who patients can see without a dentist.
question: At the chairside a patient asks you whether the dark mark on their back tooth means they need a filling, and whether they can book straight in with the hygienist next time without seeing the dentist. How should you answer each question?

teach.body: Your scope of practice is the set of tasks you have the knowledge, skills and abilities to carry out safely. The GDC's Scope of Practice guidance (from 1 November 2025) says you must only do tasks you are trained, competent and indemnified or insured to do. It has two layers: the boundaries of your registered title (what no dental nurse may do) and your personal scope (what you, individually, are trained and competent in). It grows with training and can shrink if you stop doing a task for a long time.

teach.h: Asked to do a task? Ask three questions

root.label: Am I trained, competent and indemnified?
root.sub: And is it within the dental nurse title?

children.label: Go ahead
children.sub: Under the dentist's prescription or direction

children.label: Don't do it
children.sub: Say so, check GDC guidance, ask the clinician

teach.caption: The GDC is clear: you must not be pressured into a task you don't feel trained or competent to do.

teach.h: Core role, additional skills and hard limits
head: Core role
With extra training
Never (as a nurse)
teach.caption: Core tasks come from the GDC's list for dental nurses; oral health advice and helping manage medical emergencies are also core. The GDC names only these three additional skills. Nurses can assist with whitening but never provide it.

teach.h: The hard line: no diagnosis, no treatment planning
teach.body: The GDC states plainly that dental nurses do not diagnose disease or plan treatment. You work under the prescription, direction or delegation of a dentist or another registered professional. So when a patient asks 'Do I need a filling?' or 'Which crown should I have?', the honest answer is: 'That's for the dentist to decide. Let me make sure you can ask them before you leave.' You can still give general oral health advice and explain what a procedure involves.

With further training you can add skills within the nurse boundaries. Fluoride varnish can be applied under a dentist's prescription (or patient-specific direction), often in community programmes. Taking radiographs and assisting with conscious sedation need specific training and certification set by other bodies. There must be mutual agreement with the dentist or employer that you are competent, and your indemnity must cover it. No course or CPD lets you cross into another title's work: that needs a new qualification and registration under that title.

steps.label: Check the boundaries
steps.sub: Is it allowed for a dental nurse?

steps.label: Identify training
steps.sub: In-house, or a formal assessed course

steps.label: Confirm indemnity
steps.sub: Your cover must include the task

teach.caption: The same check applies when you train a colleague: first confirm the task is within their scope.

teach.h: Direct access: who patients can see first
head: Professional
Without a dentist?
Limit
rows: IOTN screening; treatment needs a prescription
teach.caption: Tooth whitening always needs a dentist's prescription. Anyone working under direct access must refer when a patient's needs go beyond their scope.

teach.text: Training alone doesn't put a task in your scope. It must also sit within the dental nurse title. A weekend course cannot make diagnosing, prescribing or tooth whitening part of a nurse's role.

items: Scope = what you are trained, competent and indemnified to do, within your title's boundaries.
Dental nurses never diagnose or plan treatment: refer those questions to the dentist.
Additional skills (fluoride varnish, radiography, sedation nursing) need training first; some need certification.
Unsure? Don't do it. Check the GDC guidance and ask the clinician; you must not be pressured.
Direct access: hygienists and therapists (but not whitening); CDTs, dentures for patients with no natural teeth; orthodontic therapists, IOTN screening.

summary: You can now define scope of practice, use the three questions (trained, competent, indemnified) to decide whether to take on a task, name the dental nurse's core role, additional skills and hard limits, and explain who patients can see under direct access.

A.q: A patient asks you which treatment they need for a broken tooth. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Suggest the most likely treatment
Explain the dentist will discuss it
Look at the tooth and give a view
Give them a leaflet and say no more
A.why: Dental nurses do not diagnose or plan treatment. Make sure the patient can discuss it with the dentist.

whyNot.0: Suggesting treatment is treatment planning, which is outside a nurse's scope.
whyNot.2: Giving a clinical view is a form of diagnosis.
whyNot.3: A leaflet doesn't answer their question; they need to speak to the dentist.

A.q: A dental nurse wants to apply fluoride varnish. What determines whether she may do so?
options: How long she has been qualified
Whether a patient requests it
Training, competence and a prescription
Whether the practice is NHS or fully private
A.why: Fluoride varnish is an additional skill: she needs appropriate training, competence and indemnity, and it is applied under a dentist's prescription.

whyNot.0: Years of experience don't replace the specific training.
whyNot.1: A patient's request doesn't create a prescription or competence.
whyNot.3: The rules on scope are the same in NHS and private practice.

A.q: A patient rings to book a scale and polish directly with the hygienist. What does direct access allow?
options: Nothing until a dentist has examined them
Polishing only, no scaling
Any treatment including whitening
Hygienist care except tooth whitening
A.why: Under direct access a hygienist can see patients without a dentist's referral, but tooth whitening still needs a dentist's prescription.

whyNot.0: Direct access means a dentist's referral is not needed first.
whyNot.1: Scaling is well within a hygienist's scope.
whyNot.2: Tooth whitening always needs a dentist's prescription.

B.q: Which definition of 'scope of practice' is most accurate?
options: Whatever the dentist on duty asks you to do
What you are trained, competent and indemnified to do
Every task that is listed in your practice job description
Anything covered by a CPD course you have done
B.why: Scope is what you have the training, competence and indemnity to do safely, within your title's boundaries.

whyNot.0: You must not accept tasks outside your scope, even if asked.
whyNot.2: A job description can't override GDC boundaries or your competence.
whyNot.3: CPD can maintain skills but can't move you beyond your title.

B.q: A clinical dental technician wants to see a patient without a dentist's prescription. For which work is this permitted?
options: Complete dentures for patients with no teeth
Partial dentures for any patient who asks for them
Crowns and bridges on natural teeth
Custom tooth whitening trays and gel
B.why: CDTs can provide complete dentures directly to edentulous patients. Dentate patients need a referral from a dentist.

whyNot.1: Partial dentures are for dentate patients, who need a dentist's referral first.
whyNot.2: Crowns and bridges are not part of a CDT's direct access role.
whyNot.3: Whitening always needs a dentist's prescription.

B.q: You are unsure whether a task you've been asked to do falls within your role. What is the safest action?
options: Do it carefully, then mention it to the dentist after
Ask another nurse to do it for you
Check GDC guidance and ask the clinician
Refuse and leave the surgery
B.why: If unsure, don't proceed. Check the GDC guidance and discuss it with the clinician.

whyNot.0: Trying a task you may not be competent in puts patients at risk, even if you report it afterwards.
whyNot.1: Passing it on doesn't confirm the colleague is in scope either.
whyNot.3: Walking out leaves the patient and dentist unsupported; just discuss it.

C.q: The practice is introducing a new treatment you'll be assisting with. What should you establish first?
options: Whether it is in scope and what training you need
How much patients will be charged for it
Whether other nurses at the practice are already doing it
Who will be ordering the new materials
C.why: Before taking on anything new, confirm it is within your scope and identify the training you need to be competent.

whyNot.1: Fees matter to the practice, not to whether you are competent.
whyNot.2: Others doing it doesn't make you trained.
whyNot.3: Ordering is practical, but competence and scope come first.

C.q: An orthodontic therapist wants to assess a new patient without them seeing a dentist first. What may she do?
options: Fit fixed braces straight away
Carry out IOTN screening
Diagnose and plan treatment
Extract teeth to make space
C.why: Orthodontic therapists can carry out Index of Orthodontic Treatment Need screening under direct access. Treatment needs a prescription.

whyNot.0: Fitting appliances needs a prescription from a dentist.
whyNot.2: Orthodontic diagnosis and planning is for the dentist or orthodontist.
whyNot.3: Orthodontic therapists do not extract teeth.

C.q: Which task is outside the boundaries of the dental nurse title?
options: Processing radiographs
Giving oral health advice
Recording dental charting
Diagnosing caries
C.why: Dental nurses do not diagnose disease or plan treatment.

whyNot.0: Monitoring and processing images and radiographs is a core nurse task.
whyNot.1: Advising and motivating patients on oral health is core.
whyNot.2: Recording charting as the dentist dictates is core record keeping.

reteach.title: Think of a driving licence
reteach.question: A car licence lets you drive a car, not a bus, however good a driver you are. How does that match the dental nurse title and your personal skills?

blocks.body: Your GDC title is the licence: it sets the vehicle class. A dental nurse can never 'drive' diagnosis or treatment planning, just as a car licence never covers a bus. Inside that licence, your personal scope is your experience: you might be confident on motorways (radiography, after certification) but not yet towing a caravan (sedation nursing). Extra lessons add skills within the licence. Only a new test, meaning a new qualification and registration, changes the class.

blocks.h: Three layers decide what you can do

levels.label: What you personally are competent in
Boundaries of the dental nurse title

blocks.caption: Everything must sit inside the bottom layer. Training can grow the middle; only you, with honest reflection, know the top.

blocks.text: 'The dentist told me to' is not a defence. If a task is outside your scope, you must decline, even if a senior colleague asks.

explain.body: Before any task: Am I trained? Am I competent? Am I indemnified or insured? If any answer is no or unsure, don't do it. Refer, ask or arrange training.

test.q: Which question is NOT part of the GDC's check before carrying out a task?
options: Am I trained to do this?
Am I competent to do this?
Am I indemnified for this?
Am I the most senior nurse?
test.why: Seniority doesn't matter. The GDC's questions are about training, competence and indemnity.

whyNot.0: Training is one of the three questions.
whyNot.1: Competence is one of the three questions.
whyNot.2: Indemnity or insurance is one of the three questions.

explain.body: Dental nurses do not diagnose disease or plan treatment. They work under the prescription, direction or delegation of a dentist or other registered professional.

test.q: A patient asks you if the swelling in their gum is serious. What should you do?
options: Reassure them it's probably nothing
Make sure the dentist assesses it
Tell them it sounds like an abscess
Suggest they take antibiotics
test.why: Assessing the swelling is diagnosis, which is for the dentist.

whyNot.0: False reassurance is a form of diagnosis and could be wrong.
whyNot.3: Nurses don't prescribe or advise on prescription medicines.

explain.body: Fluoride varnish on prescription, taking radiographs and sedation nursing are added through training. Radiography and sedation need specific certification. You and the dentist must agree you are competent.

test.q: A newly qualified nurse is asked to take bitewing radiographs. What must be in place first?
options: Appropriate radiography training
Two years' experience
The patient's written consent
A second nurse in the room to supervise
test.why: Taking radiographs is an additional skill that needs specific training and certification.

whyNot.1: Experience alone doesn't make you competent in radiography.
whyNot.2: Consent matters, but it doesn't make an untrained nurse competent.
whyNot.3: Another nurse's presence doesn't replace your own training.

explain.body: Some professionals can see patients without a dentist's referral: hygienists and therapists (but whitening still needs a dentist's prescription), CDTs (dentures for edentulous patients) and orthodontic therapists (IOTN screening).

test.q: A patient wants to book tooth whitening directly with the therapist, without seeing a dentist. Is this allowed?
options: Yes, therapists have direct access to their full scope
Yes, if the patient signs a form
No, whitening needs a dentist's prescription
No, therapists never do whitening
test.why: Therapists can provide whitening, but only under a dentist's prescription, so it is excluded from direct access.

whyNot.0: Whitening is the exception: it always needs a dentist's prescription.
whyNot.1: A signed form doesn't replace the prescription.
whyNot.3: Therapists can whiten teeth, but on a dentist's prescription.
